title: Self-evolving LLM agents with in-distribution Optimization
claim: Prior methods suffer distribution shift and sparse-reward gaps; ours unifies reward labeling and policy learning in-distribution, with far fewer environment steps.
layout: 3 text panels left-to-right plus right scatter plot; dashed boxes, robot icons
description: The figure has two parts. On the left, three rounded dashed-border boxes sit under the headings 'With Distribution Shift Methods' and 'No Distribution Shift Methods'. The first box, 'Existing PRM pipeline', holds two blue-outlined cards. They list the costs of collecting PRM data (manual labels, discretized search states) and the two ways of improving the policy. A robot icon stands on a cliff, and orange text says 'Suffer from unseen state/actions'. The second box covers online RL, with two bullets about sparse rewards and self-play only. The third box, green and labeled 'Ours', is 'Expert + Self-Train'. It says to estimate process rewards via Bellman backup from hybrid offline data and then improve the policy. A blue feedback arrow labeled 'Self-Evolve' runs back to the data. On the right is a scatter plot of AlfWorld performance against environment steps on a log scale. Crown markers for the 1-iteration and 2-iteration versions of the method sit high and far left. The baselines SFT, QLASS and PPO sit lower or further right. An arrow connects SFT to the 1-iteration point.
caption: Comparison of existing methods. Left: Existing PRM methods rely on costly manual labels or search-based rollouts requiring discrete states, often failing due to distribution shifts between PRM training and policy improvement. Upper Mid: Most online RL does not address episodic sparse rewards. Bottom Mid: Our framework utilizes a hybrid off-policy dataset (expert + agents' interaction data) to derive rewards via Bellman backups. By co-evolving process reward supervision and policy improvement within a shared in-distribution loop, the agent achieves stable self-evolution. Right: A visualization of performance vs environment steps required for collecting data.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as powerful controllers for interactive agents in complex environments, yet training them to perform reliable long-horizon decision making remains a fundamental challenge. A key difficulty lies in credit assignment: agents often receive delayed rewards only at the end of episodes. In this paper, we propose Q-Evolve, a self-evolving framework for LLM agents that unifies automatic process-reward labeling and policy learning within a principled in-distribution reinforcement learning paradigm. In each evolving iteration, our method learns an in-distribution critic from a hybrid off-policy dataset that combines expert demonstrations with agent-generated trajectories, stabilizing Bellman backups in sparse-reward settings via a weighted Implicit Q-Learning objective. The learned value function is then used to derive step-wise process rewards through advantage estimation, enabling dense and reliable supervision without environment backtracking or human annotation. Leveraging these signals, we perform behavior-proximal policy optimization that evolves the agent over the data used for process reward labeling, allowing iterative self-improvement without exacerbating distribution shift. We evaluate our method on AlfWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, showing Q-Evolve outperforms strong baselines in sample efficiency, robustness, and overall task performance. Our results demonstrate that stable agent self-evolution is achievable through the co-evolution of process-level supervision and policy, both grounded within a shared in-distribution learning loop.
